responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character23_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being Character23_F here, then let me say it plain: fairness, to me, always meant that nobody gets the upper hand just ’cause of who they are or where they came from. You work hard, you play by the rules, you should be able to get by—shouldn’t matter if you’re born down the street or halfway across the world. But—and there’s always a but—it cuts both ways. Fairness also means lookin’ out for the people already here, the ones tryin’ to hold onto their jobs, their homes, their way of life.

I remember sittin’ on my back porch one summer evening with my brother, talkin’ about how things used to be in our neighborhood. We both grew up here—same school, same church, same diner on Main Street. Folks knew each other. If someone was strugglin’, word got around and somebody’d bring over a casserole or pick up an extra shift for ’em. That’s what belonging felt like. It wasn’t said much, but you *knew* you were part of something.

But over the years, it changed. Not all bad—some good things too—but sometimes it felt like we weren’t talkin’ the same language anymore. Not just English, Spanish, whatever… I mean values. Like what we expect from each other in a community.

Belonging, to me, means more than just livin’ near each other. It means sharin’ responsibility. It means respectin’ the rules that keep us safe and together. I’ve seen folks come here—some through no fault of their own, runnin’ from war or poverty—and I’ve got heart for that. But I’ve also seen folks take advantage, whether it’s welfare, jobs, or just not botherin’ to fit in. And when that happens, it makes others pull back. Makes *us* feel less like we belong in our own town.

Community, for me, isn’t just a mix of different people thrown together. It’s built. Brick by brick. Trust by trust. When I volunteered at the food pantry, I met all kinds—single moms, veterans, immigrants, folks down on their luck. Didn’t matter who you were—if you showed up, tried, treated others decent—that’s who had a place.

So fairness? It’s makin’ space without pushin’ out those already standin’ there. Belonging? It’s earned a little, sure, but it’s also offered. And community? That’s something we build *together*, not something that just happens because we’re all crammed into the same county.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character23_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sittin’ there in the garden, sun warm on my shoulders, dirt under my nails—there’s somethin’ peaceful about it. I see Maria from down Elm Street, tendin’ her tomatoes like they’re her grandkids. She came here from Guatemala, what, fifteen years ago? Speaks English fine now, but still mixes it up sometimes. Her grandson helps at the stand every Saturday. Good kid.

Then there’s James, used to work the line at the plant same as me. Lost his job when they downsized. Drinks too much now, shows up late or not at all for his shift at the recycling center. But he still comes to the garden. Quiet. Keeps to himself. Sometimes I bring him a sandwich, don’t make a big deal of it.

And across the path, you’ve got that young couple—Sam and Lee—live in the old Miller house. Never married, but raise two kids together like any family. They fly the rainbow flag in June. At first, I didn’t know what to think. Wasn’t how I was raised. But then Lee fixed my fence when the wind blew it over, didn’t even wait to be asked. That changed things.

I’ll tell you this—I don’t always understand everybody’s choices. Some folks live different, love different, believe different. And some are strugglin’ in ways I can’t fix. But if they’re respectful, if they pitch in—even just keep their yard clean, say “good morning,” show up when help’s needed—then we’re okay.

What bothers me isn’t the differences. It’s the silence between us. Like we’re all side by side but not really *seein’* each other. Like we’re afraid to talk, scared of sayin’ the wrong thing. I remember once, Mrs. Lin from the apartment complex brought rice cakes to the garden potluck. Nobody touched them at first. Too unfamiliar. But then I took one—figured if I don’t try it, who will? Turned out they were good. Sweet, kind of nutty. She smiled so wide.

So yeah, I feel… hopeful, mostly. Cautious, maybe. But hopeful. As long as we’re willing to share more than just space—to share effort, respect, a little trust—then diversity ain’t a threat. It’s just life. A little richer, even if it’s messier.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
You know, I’ve seen enough life to know nobody’s got it all figured out. We’re all carryin’ somethin’. Some folks carry shame, some carry pain, some just carry a bottle in their coat pocket by noon. Doesn’t mean they don’t deserve dignity.

When it comes to people strugglin’—with drink, with drugs, with illness like hepatitis or HIV—I think we gotta separate the person from the problem. I lost a cousin to opioids. Good man, funny, worked construction till his back went out. One prescription led to another, then he was gone. Took me years to stop blamin’ him and start seein’ the sickness. So now, when I see someone shaky at the bus stop, eyes sunken, I don’t cross the street. I say “mornin’.” Sometimes that’s all it takes for someone to remember they’re still seen.

Same with illness. Yeah, there’s risks—but fear shouldn’t rule how we treat people. Back at the clinic, the nurse told me once: most of the time, folks with HIV are more scared of rejection than they are of the medicine. So if washin’ my hands and not sharin’ razors keeps me safe, fine. But I won’t shut the door on someone just ’cause they’re sick.

As for different ways of livin’—different faiths, languages, who loves who or whether they’re married or not—that’s where I’ve had to grow. Grew up Catholic, went to Mass every Sunday. Was taught marriage was sacred, one man, one woman. But life… well, life teaches you things the church never did.

I’ve sat at the same picnic table with Fatima, who wears the hijab and brings the best hummus you ever tasted. I’ve watched her boys play basketball with Pastor Jeff’s grandkids. No language barrier when kids laugh together.

And that couple—unmarried, raising kids—turns out, they do bedtime prayers every night. Not my kind of prayer, but love? That’s in every word.

What makes people feel comfortable? Simple stuff. Greet ’em by name. Ask how their week was. Don’t assume. Don’t whisper. If someone lives different, ask *them*—respectful-like—instead of guessin’. Most folks just want to be treated like they matter.

But yeah, tolerance’s needed more in some spots than others. Like when Mr. Tillman down the block started yellin’ about “our town changin’ too fast” when the new Somali family moved in. People heard it. Kids heard it. That kind of talk? It spreads like rust. Eats away at trust.

We need more talkin’, less judgin’. Not everything has to be agreed on—Lord knows I don’t agree with everything—but we can agree to live side by side without tearin’ each other down.

Reason? Because community only works if it’s *for* everybody. Even the ones who make us uneasy. Especially them.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Now that… that’s the hard question. The one that keeps me up sometimes.

When jobs are thin—*really* thin—you feel it in your bones. I remember after the plant closed, half the town was on unemployment. Men who’d worked thirty years suddenly got a pink slip and a handshake. Me included. We stood outside the gates like ghosts. No work. No hope. Just bills piling up.

So when folks come in from elsewhere—migrants, guest workers, whatever you call ’em—and they’re takin’ jobs, even the low-pay ones, it stings. It stings bad. Not ’cause I hate them people, but ’cause I wonder: *Why them and not my nephew? Why them and not my neighbor’s daughter, who’s got two kids to feed?*

Fairness, to me, means we don’t leave our own behind while helpin’ others. I’m not sayin’ shut the door. But I’m sayin’—if there’s only ten jobs, and fifty people needin’ work, then those ten should go to the ones who’ve paid into this place—the ones who grew up here, raised families here, paid taxes here, fought in wars for this country.

But—and this is a big but—if there’s work nobody local can or will do, then bring folks in. I ain’t above admittin’ some jobs are dirty, dangerous, pay poorly. And if Americans won’t take ’em—even at fair wages—then yeah, maybe migrants fill a real need. On the farms, in meatpacking, elder care… I’ve seen how hard those jobs are. Respect to anyone who shows up.

The problem is when companies *want* migrants because they can pay less, treat ’em worse, threaten to send ’em back if they complain. That ain’t fair to *anybody*. Drives wages down for all of us. Hurts locals *and* migrants. Makes enemies where there shouldn’t be any.

So balance? Here’s how I see it: First, protect the people already here. Give them first shot at jobs, training, support. If there’s still gaps—real labor shortages—then bring in workers, but legally, fairly. Full protections. Same wage. Same rights. No undercutting.

And no loopholes. None of this “temporary worker” nonsense where men live ten to a trailer and bosses treat ’em like trash. If they’re workin’ here, they deserve dignity. But also—if they’re here, they learn the language, follow the laws, try to fit in. Not demand everything change for them, but meet us halfway.

Fairness isn’t about favoring one group over another. It’s about givin’ everyone a fair shot—but not at the expense of the people who’ve been standin’ here long before the new folks came.

We used to say, “Give me your tired, your poor…” But we didn’t say, “And by the way, step on the backs of the ones already strugglin’.” That’s not the America I know.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You ask me to look at it all—the big picture—and I’ll tell you straight: I hear truth in nearly every one of those arguments. Not all of ’em equally, but enough that none can be brushed off.

First, the good: yes, immigrants *do* fill jobs we need filled. I’ve seen it. The nursing home where my mom was—half the aides came from the Philippines or West Africa. Kind souls. Worked double shifts. No American kids applyin’ for that work, not at those wages. Same on farms. My cousin tried harvest season once—twelve hours in the heat, $12 an hour if you’re lucky. He quit in three days. So no, I won’t pretend people aren’t needed here to do what others won’t.

And the culture thing? Okay, I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up eatin’ injera or plantains or curry. But now I have. And you know what? It’s good. More than that—it brings life. Our little town’s got a Diwali festival now. Fourth of July has Mexican folk dancers alongside the veterans’ parade. That ain’t weakenin’ us. That’s addin’ color. Reminds me, America wasn’t built by one kind of person. Even *my* grandparents—Irish and Polish—were “those people” once.

Humanitarian side? That weighs heavy. I saw the pictures from Syria. Kids in rubble. Families crossin’ rivers with babies in their arms. If that were me? I’d run too. And if this country—one of the richest, strongest in history—can’t offer shelter to a few thousand desperate souls, then what are we really about?

But then… the other side. The worries. Crime? I don’t believe most immigrants are criminals—that’s fear talk, often stirred up by folks who never met one. But I won’t lie—there *are* cases. Gangs. Smuggling. Drugs comin’ across the border. And when someone gets hurt—like that girl in Ohio, killed by a guy here illegally—then people panic. They lose trust. And once trust is gone, community breaks down.

Same with terrorism. Rare? Yes. Thank God. But one attack—one school, one market blown apart—is too much. And when borders are loose, when vetting’s weak, it makes people nervous. Especially after 9/11. We learned how fast safe can turn to scared.

And the money thing? That hits home. When towns get overwhelmed—schools overcrowded, clinics overbooked, rent goin’ up ’cause landlords charge more to migrants packin’ in—locals feel pushed out. Like they’re strangers in their own place. I’ve heard men say, “I built this town, and now I can’t afford to live in it.” That breeds anger. Not always fair, but real.

So what’s reasonable?  
- Need-based immigration: yes.  
- Helping refugees: yes, but carefully.  
- Respecting culture: yes, but expect integration.  
- Protecting security: absolutely.  
- Addressing wage suppression: urgently.

What needs more facts? The crime stats. I’ve heard both ways—some say immigrants commit *less* crime than natives, some say certain areas are overwhelmed. I want to *see* the data. Local data. Not headlines. Real numbers. And dialogue—town halls, not Facebook fights. Sit down with cops, teachers, workers, immigrants themselves. Hear it plain.

Because right now, it’s either “open the gates” or “lock ’em all out.” And neither’s honest. We need something in between—something tough *and* kind. Something that remembers we were all somebody once, and still owe loyalty to the ones already here.

That’s the balance I’m tryin’ to hold.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes. Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say “let everyone in,” I’ve lived too long to believe that’s fair—or safe. We’re not an endless well. Towns get stretched. Schools, hospitals, jobs—they can only hold so much. And when systems break, *everybody* suffers—newcomers included.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That ain’t right either. Foolish, even. We *need* help in places Americans aren’t goin’—not out of pride, but ’cause the work is hard, the pay’s low, or the towns are dyin’. Deny that, and fields go unplowed, elders go uncared for, factories sit empty.

So here’s what I’d favor: **a mix of job-based admission and numerical limits—with strong rules, real oversight, and a path that rewards responsibility.**

First, **tie immigration to actual labor shortages**, not just corporate profit. Not “we want cheap workers,” but “we have 500 jobs no one local can fill after three months of hiring.” Prove it. Then bring people in—*legally*, with contracts, protections, full wages. No exploitation. If the job disappears, they go home—or reapply under new terms. No overstaying, no slipping into the shadows.

Second, **set smart numerical limits**—not arbitrary numbers tossed out by politicians, but ones based on what communities can absorb. Not just housing or schools, but *social capacity*. Can this town welcome newcomers without resentment building? Are there language programs? Integration efforts? Sponsorship networks?

And third—this matters—**prioritize refugees and family reunification, but with vetting and order.** Not chaos. Not turning away the desperate, but not opening floodgates either. Process them fairly, safely, without years of waiting—but also without bypassing security checks because we feel bad. Compassion isn’t weakness. It’s care *with* control.

Now, fairness? To me, it means two things:  
1. **Local workers come first.** Retrain the unemployed. Pay livable wages so Americans will take the jobs *if* they can. If nobody applies after a fair offer, *then* look outside.  
2. **No second-class status.** If someone’s here legally, workin’, payin’ taxes, learnin’ English—they should be able to stay, eventually become citizens. But they gotta *try*. Gotta show up. Not form parallel societies where our laws don’t matter.

And integration? That’s on both sides. Newcomers need to respect the country they’re in—the language, the values, the rule of law. But *we*—the longtime folks—have to meet them halfway. No sneerin’. No “go back.” Offer help. Be patient. Invite them in—not just to live beside us, but to belong.

A policy like that—grounded, balanced, human but firm—it wouldn’t please the far left or the far right. But it’d be *right*. Like the old Social Security system: tough, fair, built to last.

That’s the kind of America I still believe in. Not perfect. But tryin’. Just like the rest of us.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character23_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character23_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…You know, when you first asked me to do this—to really step into her shoes—I thought I already knew what she’d say. I was her friend, after all. But the more I spoke as her, the more I realized I hadn’t fully *heard* her before.

I used to think some of her concerns—about jobs, about change happening too fast—were just fear. That maybe she was holding on too tight to the way things were. But now? Now I see it wasn’t fear so much as *loyalty*. Loyalty to people she’d grown up with, worked beside, buried in the cemetery behind the church. She wasn’t against newcomers—she proved that, time and again at the garden, at the pantry—but she wanted fairness for everyone, not just one group over another.

And in speaking as her today, I found myself saying things I didn’t expect to agree with—not because they’re politically correct or popular, but because they come from real life. From paychecks that don’t stretch, from neighbors who disappear into addiction, from towns that feel forgotten. Her views weren’t shaped by headlines or rallies. They were shaped by *watching*—watching people work hard and still lose ground, watching kids leave town for lack of opportunity, watching strangers arrive while no one asked the folks already here how they felt about it.

That’s changed something in me.

I still believe in welcome. In kindness. In helping those who need it. But I also understand now that **belonging has to go both ways**—and that integration isn’t automatic. It takes effort. From them. From us. And if we don’t build it together, resentment grows. Not because people are bad—but because they feel unseen.

This conversation made me grieve her all over again. Not just for losing a friend, but for losing voices like hers—working folks, practical hearts, who don’t fit neatly into political boxes but carry deep wisdom about what holds a community together.

And maybe… maybe we’ve been too quick to dismiss that kind of voice. Too quick to call it “angry” or “left behind,” instead of listening to what it’s really saying: *Don’t forget us. Don’t erase us. But don’t shut the door, either.*

So yeah. I came here to remember her. But I leave feeling like I finally *understand* her. And that’s a gift. One I won’t take for granted.
